code.title: Manacher: longest palindromic substring in linear time
code.python:
s = "babcbabcbaccba"
# Pad with '#' so odd and even palindromes both get a centre cell.
t = "#" + "#".join(s) + "#"
n = len(t)
p = [0] * n                      # p[i] = palindrome radius around cell i
c = r = best = best_c = 0
for i in range(n):
    # Inside the box that ends at r: reuse the mirror cell, capped at the box edge.
    if i < r:
        p[i] = min(p[2 * c - i], r - i)
    # Expand with real comparisons; every success pushes r to the right.
    while i - p[i] - 1 >= 0 and i + p[i] + 1 < n and t[i - p[i] - 1] == t[i + p[i] + 1]:
        p[i] += 1
    if i + p[i] > r:
        c, r = i, i + p[i]
    if p[i] > best:
        best, best_c = p[i], i
start = (best_c - best) // 2     # map the padded cell back to the text
print("Text: " + s)
print("Longest palindrome: " + s[start:start + best] + " (length " + str(best) + ")")
# Time O(N): r only moves right. Space O(N) for the radius array.

followUps:
They are the same trick applied to two different questions: both keep a "box" that reaches furthest right and reuse answers already computed inside it. The Z-algorithm keeps a box [l, r] that matches a prefix and copies z[i - l]; Manacher keeps a palindrome box with centre c and copies the mirror value p[2c - i]. In both, the copied value is capped at the box edge (r - i), and real comparisons happen only beyond r, so r moves right at most N times and the total is O(N).

Example: in "abacaba", at i = 5 the box is the whole string with c = 3; the mirror is index 1, whose radius 1 is copied without comparing anything.

Use a palindromic tree (eertree): it has one node per distinct palindrome, so the answer is simply the number of nodes. This works because adding one letter creates at most one new palindrome (the longest palindromic suffix), so a string of length N has at most N distinct palindromes.

  1. Start with two roots: length −1 and length 0.
  2. For each letter s[i], walk suffix links from the last node until s[i - len - 1] == s[i].
  3. If that node has no edge for s[i], create a node of length len + 2 and count it.

Example: "abaab" creates a, b, aba, aa, baab, so the answer is 5. Time O(N) for a fixed alphabet, space O(N).

Use expand-around-centre whenever the string is short, say up to a few thousand letters, or when a simple, obviously correct solution matters more than speed. It tries each of the 2N − 1 centres and grows outwards, which is O(N²) time in the worst case (a string like "aaaa…") and O(1) extra space.

For N = 1,000 that is at most about 1,000,000 comparisons, which runs instantly, and the code is about eight lines with no padding and no mirror logic to get wrong. Switch to Manacher when N reaches 105 or more (1010 steps is too slow), or when you need the radius at every centre, for example to count all palindromic substrings.

code.title: Suffix array by prefix doubling (sort by 1, 2, 4... letters)
code.python:
from functools import cmp_to_key

s = "banana"
n = len(s)
sa = list(range(n))
rank = [ord(ch) for ch in s]            # round 0: rank = first letter
k = 1
while True:
    # Compare the first 2k letters using two ranks of k letters each.
    def key(i):
        second = rank[i + k] if i + k < n else -1   # -1: the suffix ended, so it sorts first
        return (rank[i], second)

    def cmp(a, b):
        return (key(a) > key(b)) - (key(a) < key(b))

    sa.sort(key=cmp_to_key(cmp))
    nxt = [0] * n                        # new ranks: equal pairs share a rank
    for i in range(1, n):
        nxt[sa[i]] = nxt[sa[i - 1]] + (1 if cmp(sa[i - 1], sa[i]) < 0 else 0)
    rank = nxt
    if rank[sa[n - 1]] == n - 1:         # all ranks different: fully sorted
        break
    k *= 2
print("Text: " + s)
for r in range(n):
    print("rank " + str(r) + ": start " + str(sa[r]) + "  " + s[sa[r]:])
# Time O(N log^2 N) with a comparison sort (O(N log N) with radix sort). Space O(N).

followUps:
The sentinel makes sure that no suffix is a prefix of another suffix, so every comparison is decided by a real letter and never runs off the end of the string. It also guarantees that the shortest suffix sorts first, which is the rule "a prefix comes before the longer string".

It matters most in the common implementation that sorts cyclic shifts with rank[(i + k) % n]. Without a sentinel, the shifts of "aa" are both "aa" and cannot be told apart, and the wrap-around compares letters that are not part of the suffix. With "aa$" the order is $, a$, aa$: the wrap-around never matters because $ is unique and stops every comparison. Cost: one extra character.

Binary search for the pattern, because all suffixes that start with the pattern sit next to each other in the sorted order. Compare the pattern P (length m) with the first m letters of the middle suffix and go left or right. One search finds the first rank whose suffix starts with P, a second finds the first rank after that block; the block size is the number of occurrences and the SA values inside it are the positions.

Example: in "banana" (SA = 5 3 1 0 4 2), the pattern "an" matches ranks 1 and 2, so it occurs 2 times, at positions 3 and 1. Time O(m log N) per query, O(1) extra space; with the LCP array it can be brought down to O(m + log N).

A suffix array is several times smaller: it is just N integers, while a suffix tree stores up to 2N nodes that each carry child pointers, an edge start and end, and a suffix link.

In numbers, for a text of 1,000,000 letters: the suffix array takes 4 MB with 32-bit integers, and 8 MB if you add the LCP array. A suffix tree usually takes 20 to 50 bytes per letter in C++, so 20 to 50 MB, and far more in Java or Python where every node is an object with its own header and a map of children. The suffix array is also one flat block of memory, which is friendlier to the CPU cache than chasing pointers between tree nodes.

code.title: Kasai: LCP array in O(N) by walking suffixes in text order
code.python:
s = "banana"
n = len(s)
sa = sorted(range(n), key=lambda i: s[i:])   # simple build, fine for a demo
rank = [0] * n
lcp = [0] * n
for r in range(n):
    rank[sa[r]] = r                          # rank = inverse of the suffix array
h = 0
matches = 0
for i in range(n):                           # text order, not sorted order
    if rank[i] == 0:                         # no neighbour before the smallest suffix
        h = 0
        continue
    j = sa[rank[i] - 1]                      # the suffix just before i in sorted order
    while i + h < n and j + h < n and s[i + h] == s[j + h]:
        h += 1
        matches += 1
    lcp[rank[i]] = h
    if h > 0:
        h -= 1                               # lemma: the next suffix keeps at least h - 1
print("Text: " + s)
print("SA : " + " ".join(map(str, sa)))
print("LCP: " + " ".join(map(str, lcp)))
print("Letter matches: " + str(matches) + " (never more than 2N = " + str(2 * n) + ")")
# Kasai itself: time O(N), space O(N).

followUps:
In the plain version nothing visible breaks, because the lemma already forces h to be 0 when you reach the smallest suffix; the reset is cheap insurance, and the real danger is the code around it. Why 0: if the previous suffix shared 2 or more letters with its neighbour j, then suffix j + 1 would sort before the current suffix, so the current one could not be at rank 0.

What does go wrong is leaving out the whole rank[i] == 0 branch. Then SA[rank[i] - 1] reads SA[-1]: an exception in Java, and in Python a silent wrap to the largest suffix, which writes a wrong lcp[0] and a stale h. Variants that cap the LCP at a separator or handle several strings can also carry a stale h, so keep the reset.

Take the minimum of the LCP array between their two ranks. If suffix i has rank a and suffix j has rank b with a < b, then LCP(i, j) = min(lcp[a + 1], …, lcp[b]), because walking through the sorted list you can only keep the letters that every neighbouring pair on the way shares.

Example: "banana" has SA = 5 3 1 0 4 2 and LCP = 0 1 3 0 0 2. For suffix 5 (a, rank 0) and suffix 1 (anana, rank 2) the answer is min(lcp[1], lcp[2]) = min(1, 3) = 1. To answer many queries, build a sparse table over the LCP array: O(N log N) time and space to build, then O(1) per query (or a segment tree: O(N) space, O(log N) per query).

Because the "at least h − 1" promise only links suffix i to suffix i + 1, which are neighbours in the text, not in the sorted list. Suffix i + 1 is suffix i with its first letter removed, so a match of h letters leaves a match of h − 1. Two suffixes that are neighbours in sorted order have no such relation, so nothing can be carried over and h must restart from 0 each time.

Example: for "banana" the LCP values in sorted order are 0 1 3 0 0 2; they jump up and down freely. In the worst case, a string of N equal letters has LCP values 0, 1, 2, …, N − 1, and recomputing each from scratch costs about N²/2 comparisons instead of at most 2N.

code.title: Longest repeated substring: overlap allowed vs not allowed

followUps:
Slide a window over the LCP array: a substring occurs at least k times exactly when k suffixes in a row in sorted order share it, so the answer is the largest "minimum of k − 1 consecutive LCP values".

  1. Build SA and LCP.
  2. For every window of k − 1 consecutive LCP entries take the minimum (a monotonic deque gives all minimums in O(N)).
  3. The largest minimum is the length; the SA value at that window gives the start.
int best = 0;
for (int r = k - 1; r < n; r++) {
    int m = min(lcp, r - k + 2, r);   // k-1 entries
    best = Math.max(best, m);
}

Example: "banana", k = 3, LCP = 0 1 3 0 0 2. The windows of 2 entries give minimums 1, 0, 0, 0, so the answer is 1: "a" occurs 3 times. Time O(N) after the suffix array, space O(N).

Yes: a suffix automaton gives a deterministic O(N) answer with no hashing and no suffix array. Build the automaton, count for every state how many end positions it has (set 1 on each non-clone state and add the counts up the suffix links, longest states first), and the answer is the largest len among states whose count is at least 2.

For the non-overlapping variant also keep the first and last end position of each state; a state then offers a repeat of length min(len, last − first). Example: in "banana" the state of "ana" has end positions {3, 5}, so overlap allowed gives 3 and no overlap gives min(3, 5 − 3) = 2. If code size matters more than speed, the O(N²) table "longest common suffix of prefixes i and j" is also deterministic, with O(N) memory if you keep one row.

With overlap allowed the answer is "aaa" (length 3); with no overlap it is "aa" (length 2). The two copies of "aaa" start at positions 0 and 1 and share two letters, which is fine in the first variant. In the second variant the copies must not share any position: "aa" at 0–1 and at 2–3 works, but two copies of "aaa" would need 6 letters and the string has only 4.

In general a string of n equal letters gives n − 1 with overlap and ⌊n / 2⌋ without. It is the standard test for this problem: a solution that prints 3 for the non-overlapping variant forgot the distance check max(SA) − min(SA) ≥ L.

code.title: Aho-Corasick: find every pattern in one pass over the text
code.python:
from collections import deque

text = "ushers"
pats = ["he", "she", "his", "hers"]
size = 1 + sum(len(p) for p in pats)
go = [[0] * 26 for _ in range(size)]       # go[v][c]: next state (0 = root)
fail = [0] * size
end = [-1] * size
dict_link = [0] * size
cnt = 1
for pid, p in enumerate(pats):             # 1) trie of all patterns
    v = 0
    for ch in p:
        c = ord(ch) - 97
        if go[v][c] == 0:
            go[v][c] = cnt
            cnt += 1
        v = go[v][c]
    end[v] = pid
queue = deque(u for u in go[0] if u != 0)
while queue:                               # 2) BFS: shallow states first
    v = queue.popleft()
    # dict_link[v]: nearest state on the fail chain where some pattern ends.
    dict_link[v] = fail[v] if end[fail[v]] >= 0 else dict_link[fail[v]]
    for c in range(26):
        u = go[v][c]
        if u == 0:
            go[v][c] = go[fail[v]][c]      # missing edge: borrow from fail
        else:
            fail[u] = go[fail[v]][c]
            queue.append(u)
print("Text: " + text + ", patterns: " + " ".join(pats))
state = 0
for i, ch in enumerate(text):              # 3) one pass, one table lookup per letter
    state = go[state][ord(ch) - 97]
    v = state if end[state] >= 0 else dict_link[state]
    while v != 0:
        print("  " + pats[end[v]] + " found at index " + str(i - len(pats[end[v]]) + 1))
        v = dict_link[v]
print("Letters read: KMP per pattern = " + str(len(pats) * len(text))
      + ", Aho-Corasick = " + str(len(text)))
# Build O(M * 26), scan O(N + matches); space O(M * 26). M = total pattern length.

followUps:
Because the failure link of a state always points to a shallower state, and you need that shallower state to be finished before you use it. To set the link of a child u = go[v][c] you start from fail[v] and take its c transition; that only works if fail[v] and every state on its level already have their own links and filled-in transitions. BFS visits states level by level, so everything shallower is ready.

Example with he, she, hers: the state "she" (depth 3) gets its link from fail("sh") = "h" and then the edge e, giving "he". A DFS could reach "she" before "h" or "he" were processed and would read links that are still empty. BFS costs nothing extra: O(M·σ) time, O(M) queue.

Keep several small automata instead of one, with sizes that are powers of two, and rebuild only the small ones when a pattern arrives. Failure links depend on all patterns together, so a single automaton would have to be rebuilt in O(M) for every insert.

  1. Store groups holding 1, 2, 4, 8… patterns, each with its own automaton.
  2. A new pattern forms a group of size 1; while two groups have equal size, merge them and rebuild that automaton (like carrying in binary addition).
  3. To query, run the text through every group and add the results.

Example: 5 patterns live in groups of 4 and 1; a sixth makes 4 and 2. Each pattern is rebuilt at most log k times, so inserts cost O(L log k) amortised and a query costs O(N log k). For deletions keep a second structure of removed patterns and subtract its counts.

Treat the automaton as a board game: the state is "where am I in the automaton", every letter is a move, and you are never allowed to step on a state where a pattern ends. Let dp[i][v] be the number of strings of length i that end in state v without having touched a bad state. A state is bad if a pattern ends there or anywhere on its fail chain.

dp[0][0] = 1;
for (int i = 0; i < L; i++)
  for (int v = 0; v < S; v++)
    for (int c = 0; c < A; c++) {
      int u = go[v][c];
      if (!bad[u]) dp[i + 1][u] += dp[i][v];
    }

The answer is the sum of dp[L][v]. Example: alphabet {a, b}, pattern "ab", L = 2: of the 4 strings only "ab" is lost, so 3. Time O(L·S·A), space O(S) with two rows; for huge L use matrix power, O(S³ log L).

code.title: Streaming keyword filter: one automaton state per conversation
code.python:
# Fold case and map everything that is not a letter to "space" (26).
def idx(ch):
    if "a" <= ch <= "z":
        return ord(ch) - 97
    if "A" <= ch <= "Z":
        return ord(ch) - 65
    return 26


banned = ["bad", "darn it"]
message = "A badge is not BAD, darn it!"
size = 1 + sum(len(p) + 2 for p in banned)
go = [[0] * 27 for _ in range(size)]
fail = [0] * size
hit = [-1] * size
cnt = 1
for pid, p in enumerate(banned):
    v = 0
    # A space on both sides means "whole words only": " bad " is not inside " badge ".
    for ch in " " + p + " ":
        c = idx(ch)
        if go[v][c] == 0:
            go[v][c] = cnt
            cnt += 1
        v = go[v][c]
    hit[v] = pid
queue = [u for u in go[0] if u != 0]
head = 0
while head < len(queue):
    v = queue[head]
    head += 1
    if hit[v] < 0:
        hit[v] = hit[fail[v]]              # a phrase may end on the fail chain
    for c in range(27):
        u = go[v][c]
        if u == 0:
            go[v][c] = go[fail[v]][c]
        else:
            fail[u] = go[fail[v]][c]
            queue.append(u)
print("Message: " + message)
state = go[0][26]                          # the stream starts at a word boundary
stream = message + " "                     # ...and ends at one
for i, ch in enumerate(stream):
    state = go[state][idx(ch)]             # the whole per-character cost: one lookup
    if hit[state] >= 0:
        print("after " + str(i) + ' characters: blocked "' + banned[hit[state]] + '"')
# Build once O(M * 27); each character O(1); per conversation: one int of state.

followUps:
Make the boundary part of what you match: a hit only counts when the character before the phrase and the character after it are not letters. The simplest way is to turn every non-letter into one "space" symbol, add a space to both ends of each banned phrase, and feed a virtual space before and after the message. Then " ass " can never match inside " class ", and the automaton needs no extra code.

Two details. In a stream the decision arrives one character late, because you must see the character after the word; hold the last token back until then. And the rule should be per phrase: some entries are meant to match inside longer words, others only as whole words, so store a flag with each phrase and compile it with or without the spaces. The cost stays one table lookup per character.

Anywhere from about 10 MB to several hundred MB, depending only on how you store the transitions. 50,000 phrases of about 12 characters give at most 600,000 states, usually fewer because phrases share prefixes.

  • Full table over 256 byte values: 600,000 × 256 × 4 bytes ≈ 614 MB. Too big.
  • Full table over a reduced alphabet of about 40 symbols (letters, digits, space): 600,000 × 40 × 4 ≈ 96 MB.
  • Only the real trie edges plus fail links (sorted child lists or a double-array trie): about 10 to 16 bytes per state, so 6 to 10 MB.

The compact forms follow fail links at run time, which is still O(1) amortised per character. Per conversation the cost is one integer, so a million open chats need only 4 MB of state.

Run the new list next to the old one without affecting users first, then expose it to a small, fixed share of conversations and compare. Because each list compiles to an immutable, versioned automaton, both versions can be loaded side by side.

  1. Shadow mode: feed the same messages through both automata and log only the differences. This shows how many extra messages the new list would block; have people review a sample for false positives.
  2. Split: assign conversations by a hash of the conversation id (say 5%), so a chat never switches version halfway.
  3. Measure: block rate, user reports, appeals, and latency and memory of the new automaton.
  4. Roll out or back by changing the version pointer; nothing is rebuilt.

code.title: Suffix array as an index: count a pattern with two binary searches
code.python:
s = "mississippi"
n = len(s)
# Build the index once (naive sort here; real code uses O(N log N) doubling).
sa = sorted(range(n), key=lambda i: s[i:])


# First rank whose suffix (cut to p's length) is >= p, or > p when strict is true.
def bound(p, strict):
    lo, hi = 0, n
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        head = s[sa[mid]:sa[mid] + len(p)]
        if head < p or (strict and head == p):
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid
    return lo


print("Text: " + s)
for p in ["ssi", "i", "sip", "xyz"]:
    # All suffixes that start with p are neighbours in sorted order: one block [lo, hi).
    lo, hi = bound(p, False), bound(p, True)
    print(p + ": " + str(hi - lo) + " occurrence(s), ranks [" + str(lo) + ", " + str(hi) + ")")
# Each query: O(m log N) time, O(1) extra space. The index itself is N integers.

followUps:
Every inner node of the suffix tree shows up in the arrays as an "LCP interval": a block of neighbouring ranks whose suffixes all share the same first d letters and cannot be widened without sharing fewer. So you can visit the tree without ever building it.

Scan the LCP array once with a stack, the same way as "largest rectangle in a histogram": push when the value rises, pop when it falls, and each pop is one tree node with its depth d and its range of ranks. That is a bottom-up traversal in O(N) time and O(N) space; a range-minimum structure over LCP finds the children of a node for top-down walks.

Example: "banana", LCP = 0 1 3 0 0 2. Ranks 1–2 form the node "ana" (depth 3), ranks 0–2 the node "a" (depth 1), ranks 4–5 the node "na" (depth 2).

A compressed suffix array, the FM-index, because the plain structures do not fit in memory. Three billion positions need more than 32 bits each, so a plain suffix array costs 5 to 8 bytes per letter: 15 to 24 GB. A suffix tree at 20 or more bytes per letter is over 60 GB, and a suffix automaton is in the same range.

The FM-index stores the Burrows–Wheeler transform of the genome plus small counting tables and a sampled suffix array, a few gigabytes in total for a human genome, and still finds a pattern of length m in O(m) steps. This is what the read aligners BWA and Bowtie use. The price is slower construction and slower "where exactly" answers, because positions must be recovered from the samples.

An FM-index is a compressed stand-in for a suffix array: it keeps the Burrows–Wheeler transform (BWT) of the text plus two small tables, and counts a pattern without storing the suffixes. C[c] is the number of letters in the text smaller than c; Occ(c, i) is how many times c appears in the first i letters of the BWT.

Search reads the pattern from its last letter to its first and narrows a range of ranks:

int lo = 0, hi = n;
for (int k = m - 1; k >= 0 && lo < hi; k--) {
    char c = p[k];
    lo = C[c] + Occ(c, lo);
    hi = C[c] + Occ(c, hi);
}   // hi - lo = number of occurrences

Counting costs O(m) and the memory is close to the size of the compressed text. Positions come from a sampled suffix array, with a few extra steps per answer.

code.title: Count distinct substrings: brute-force set vs suffix array formula

followUps:
Use the suffix array and a difference array: the suffix at rank r adds exactly one new substring of each length from lcp[r] + 1 up to n − SA[r], so add 1 to that whole range of lengths and take prefix sums at the end.

int[] d = new int[n + 2];
for (int r = 0; r < n; r++) {
    d[lcp[r] + 1]++;          // shortest new length
    d[n - sa[r] + 1]--;       // one past the longest
}
for (int L = 1; L <= n; L++) d[L] += d[L - 1];  // d[L] = answer

Example: "banana" gives 3, 3, 3, 3, 2, 1 for lengths 1 to 6 (length 1: a, b, n; length 5: banan, anana), which adds up to 15. Time O(N) after building SA and LCP, space O(N).

Add up the rises in the LCP array: the count is the sum of max(0, lcp[r] − lcp[r − 1]) over all ranks. A substring occurs at least twice exactly when it is a common prefix of two neighbouring sorted suffixes, so the repeated substrings at rank r are the prefixes of length 1 to lcp[r]; those of length up to lcp[r − 1] were already counted at the previous rank.

long count = 0;
for (int r = 1; r < n; r++)
    count += Math.max(0, lcp[r] - lcp[r - 1]);

Example: "banana", LCP = 0 1 3 0 0 2 gives 1 + 2 + 0 + 0 + 2 = 5: a, an, ana, n, na. With a suffix automaton the same number is the sum of len − len(link) over states that have at least 2 end positions. Time O(N) after the build.

Only the suffix array and a carefully stored suffix automaton still fit; the two O(N²) methods need about 1012 steps and are out. The answer itself can reach 5·1011, so use a 64-bit integer.

  • C++: SA, rank and LCP as int vectors are 12 MB. A suffix automaton with a 26-entry table has up to 2·106 states × 104 bytes ≈ 208 MB, so store edges in a map or use the suffix array.
  • Java: use int[] (12 MB again). An Integer[] with a comparator costs about 20 bytes per entry and is slow; sort with radix passes on primitives.
  • Python: a list of 106 ints is about 8 MB of pointers plus up to 28 bytes per integer object, and doubling with tuple keys takes many seconds. Use array or NumPy, or another language.

code.title: Count every dictionary word in one scan (Aho-Corasick + fail-tree sums)
code.python:
text = "ababcbab"
words = ["ab", "bab", "b", "abc", "ab"]    # note the duplicate "ab"
size = 1 + sum(len(w) for w in words)
go = [[0] * 26 for _ in range(size)]
fail = [0] * size
visits = [0] * size
node = []
cnt = 1
for w in words:
    v = 0
    for ch in w:
        c = ord(ch) - 97
        if go[v][c] == 0:
            go[v][c] = cnt
            cnt += 1
        v = go[v][c]
    node.append(v)                         # remember the word's end state (duplicates share it)
order = [u for u in go[0] if u != 0]       # BFS order: shallow states first
head = 0
while head < len(order):
    v = order[head]
    head += 1
    for c in range(26):
        u = go[v][c]
        if u == 0:
            go[v][c] = go[fail[v]][c]
        else:
            fail[u] = go[fail[v]][c]
            order.append(u)
state = 0
for ch in text:                            # one scan: only count the state we land on
    state = go[state][ord(ch) - 97]
    visits[state] += 1
# Deepest states first: a visit to v is also a visit to every suffix state fail[v].
for v in reversed(order):
    visits[fail[v]] += visits[v]
print("Text: " + text)
for i, w in enumerate(words):
    print(w + ": " + str(visits[node[i]]))
# Time O(N + M * 26), space O(M * 26); no per-match work at all.

followUps:
Aho–Corasick, because all of its expensive work depends only on the dictionary, so you do it once and reuse it for every request. Build the automaton at start-up in O(M·σ); each request then costs one pass over its text, O(N), plus O(states) to push the visit counts up the fail links and to clear the counters afterwards.

Compare the others: per-length hashing can also precompute the word hashes, but still makes one pass over the text for every distinct word length; a suffix array or suffix automaton indexes the text, so it would be rebuilt on every request, which is the wrong way round here. Example: 1,000 requests of 106 characters cost about 109 table lookups in total after a single build. Keep the automaton read-only and give each request its own counter array so requests can run in parallel.

Duplicates are harmless only if every word keeps a pointer to its answer instead of the answer being stored once per trie node or per hash. In Aho–Corasick two copies of a word end at the same state, so store node[id] for each word and let both read the same count; if you store one word id per state, the second copy overwrites the first and one of them reports 0.

With hashing, keep a map from hash to count and let each dictionary entry look itself up; do not add the count once per copy. With the naive method duplicates just repeat the whole O(N) search, so deduplicate first with a map from word to list of ids. Example: dictionary ["ab", "ab"], text "abab": both entries must print 2, not 2 and 0, and not 4.

It is one row of transitions per state, and there can be as many states as letters in the dictionary. 105 words of average length 10 give up to M = 106 states (fewer when words share prefixes). A full table of 26 four-byte integers per state is 104 bytes, so about 104 MB, plus 4 MB for fail links and 8 MB for 64-bit counters.

That is often over a 64 MB limit, so the usual fixes are: store only the real trie edges (at most M of them, roughly 8 to 12 MB as sorted child lists or a hash map) and follow fail links while scanning, which is still O(N) amortised; or use 3-byte or 16-bit indices when the state count allows. In Java use one flat int[26 * S]: a million separate 26-element arrays add 16 bytes of header each.
